text: Does lipedema increase the prevalence of joint hypermobility?
minor_problems: [minor] P2: not fully supported — suggested: Joint hypermobility is reported more often in women with lipedema than in comparison groups, though comparisons are observational and may be confounded. propositions.statement: Joint hypermobility is frequently reported among women with lipedema.
propositions.rationale: Several reviews and a guideline report high crude prevalence of hypermobility in lipedema without comparison groups.

evidence.finding: Review states generalized joint hypermobility is present in at least 50% of women with lipedema, possibly increasing joint loading and knee pain.
Review citing a prior study of 160 lipedema patients reports joint hypermobility in over 50%, noted as a risk factor for joint disease and aortic stiffness.
US standard-of-care consensus guideline lists joint hypermobility in about 50% of women with lipedema as a comorbidity, consistent with hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

Ultrasound study of fascial remodeling included participants with both hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and lipedema; lipedema types and stages matched prior data, without testing whether lipedema raises hypermobility prevalence.

propositions.statement: Joint hypermobility is reported more often in lipedema than in comparison groups in unadjusted observational comparisons.
propositions.rationale: Comparative observational data show higher hypermobility in lipedema than in lymphedema patients or controls, without adjustment.

evidence.finding: Cross-sectional online survey: lipedema patients reported hypermobility more often than lymphedema patients (44% in adulthood, about 60% in childhood), plus joint pain and multisystem symptoms.
Narrative review compiles Beighton-positive hypermobility in 31.59% (n=232), dislocations/sprains 20.9%, and an odds ratio for joint hypermobility of 12.88 versus controls.

propositions.statement: Observational evidence has not established whether joint hypermobility is an intrinsic feature of lipedema or present only in patient subsets.
propositions.rationale: A review cautions that hypermobility reports come from subsets and observational data that cannot establish intrinsic association.

evidence.finding: Narrative review notes hypermobility, instability and biomechanical dysfunction reported in subsets of lipedema patients, but concludes observational evidence does not establish whether these features are intrinsic to lipedema.

verdicts.note: E3, E5, E6 consistently report about 50% or more; all are secondary/review sources, but the wording 'frequently reported' fits. E4 correctly context.

verdicts.suggested_statement: Joint hypermobility is reported more often in women with lipedema than in comparison groups, though comparisons are observational and may be confounded.
verdicts.note: E1 (vs lymphedema) and E2 (OR vs controls, via a narrative review) support a comparison; 'unadjusted' is not stated in the items and E2 also includes non-comparative figures (31.59% Beighton-positive). Only one primary comparison is directly visible.

verdicts.suggested_statement: Whether joint hypermobility is intrinsic to lipedema remains unestablished, since observational reports come from patient subsets.
verdicts.note: E7 supports the caveat but the wording 'or present only in patient subsets' is muddled; single review source.
